Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
As has been noted, many players were apparently not inspired to play to
win on day 1 of the NAC, due entirely to the fact that counting the
number of players led to the conclusion that a top-40 finish would be
achieved with only 3 VPs over the three rounds, and might be achieved
with only 2 VPs.

Options to remedy that:

1) Don't make 40 the fixed cutoff line. Take only 25 or 30 or 35,
depending on the participation level.

2) Count GWs on day 1 as additional VPs on day 2 (making every GW
important again). That is, a player with 2GWs and 9VPs on day 1 and 1GW
and 4VPs on day 2 is counted as 1GW 6VPs for purposes of getting into
the finals of day 2.

3) Day 1 is an unsanctioned elimination tournament, but in reverse.
After the first round, all players with game wins qualify for day 2 and
are removed from the remainder of day 1. Continue until 30 players make
the cut, and take an additional 0 to 4 players (the top-scoring
no-GW-getting players) as needed to make day 2 a multiple of five. This
has the daunting problem of determining seating, since seating cannot
be made until a round is entirely over, and would have to be done by
hand.

4) Make a single 5+F tournament, spread over 2 days. Again a bit of a
seating problem creeps in. And the kingmaking aspect of being
eliminated from the finals before round 5 begins. Plus the unfun aspect
of playing the same deck five times in a row.

Thoughts on these? Other ideas?

Messages.Body:
> I currently prefer the idea of a 5+F tournament.

I guess my opinion is sort of irrelevent, since I've never attended
these events, but I really don't like that idea. In a 3 round
tournaments it's often the case that as of round 3 (or even round 2)
you know for a fact you can't win the tournament. Knowing that as of
round 3 in a 5 round structure would be horrible. I haven't really
crunched the numbers to figure out how likely it is to be totally
shafted that early and have to keep playing multiple games to win
(which you can't). I'm not sure how adding more rounds fixes any of the
problems with large tournaments.

> Another possible (additional?) idea: Elimination of
> the withdrawal rule.

This actually strikes me as something to seriously consider. It
seriously hampers VP deals, makes Twister slightly less stupid, and
doesn't get in the way of much else. I mean, I have seen people
successfully withdraw when their library was depleted just to salvage a
VP, but I haven't seen it often. Getting rid of the obnoxious table
talk about VP deals would certainly be worth losing the occasional use
of the withdrawal rule as it was intended.

Of course, Brinkmanship becomes a dead card, but does anyone really
care?

Messages.Author: John Flournoy
Messages.Body:
LSJ wrote:

> Thoughts on these? Other ideas?

Another option that was brought up last year:

Play 3 rounds as normal using Archon.

After 3 rounds, the top 25 are seated for a 'semi-final' round. That
seating could be completely random, or even semi-seeded (for instance,
splitting the tables 1-7-13-19-25, 2-8-14-20-22, 3-9-15-16-22,
4-10-11-17-23, 5-6-12-18-24, and then randomizing seating and 1st turn
at each table).

The 5 best results strictly from the semi-final round advance to the
final. This would mean that if each SF table produces a GW, those GWers
would be the finalists. If less than 5 game wins are produced, the seat
would go to the most VP in the semi-final, breaking ties by the overall
standing of round 1-3.

(Example: Semifinal table 1 is split 3-2 between A and B; semifinal 2
is a 2-2-1 split between C D and E. All other tables are 5VP sweeps.
Advancing would be the sweepers, player A for his GW, and whichever
player of B, C, and D was the highest-placed going into the
semi-final.)

This would encourage players to play for a GW in the semi-final, and to
maximize their standing in 1-3 as well - you could play to 'just make
the semi-final' with a mediocre result, but you'd be handicapped by
facing stronger decks and needing a GW in the semi-final round if you
do that.

Downside: The finalists would be playing their decks 5 times, but then
hey, they're getting nice prizes for making the final table already.

-John Flournoy

OK Chances are I'll never get to play in this event, but I'll throw out
some suggestions for general consumption.

> Options to remedy that:
>
> 1) Don't make 40 the fixed cutoff line. Take only 25 or 30 or 35,

IMHO, participation level should always be reflected in the numbers of
a 2 day event. What happens if in one year you get 120 players and the
next 40? (Highly unlikely I know) Perhaps a baseline of 50% of
attendee's with the option of adding a few more players if the
qualifying number is not divisible by 5? That way at least you
encourage more competition on day one and a GW become more desireable
for everyone

> 2) Count GWs on day 1 as additional VPs on day 2 (making every GW
> important again). That is, a player with 2GWs and 9VPs on day 1 and 1GW
> and 4VPs on day 2 is counted as 1GW 6VPs for purposes of getting into
> the finals of day 2.
>

This sounds very similar to a 5R+Final event, just with a slight
variation (partial re-start on day 2). It would push the competative
level of the first day up as people want to walk into day 2 with a
clear advantage based on their performance on day 1. This idea, IMHO,
would make the best "compromise" in terms of wanting to push day one
competition levels without totally hosing someone who happens to have a
bad day. It also allows for a change of deck at the midpoint if desired
(or enforced), which a 2 day, 5R+Final, event pretty much procludes.
Without instituting major changes, this option is probably your best
bet for increasing pure competition on day one.

> 3) Day 1 is an unsanctioned elimination tournament, but in reverse.
> After the first round, all players with game wins qualify for day 2 and
> are removed from the remainder of day 1. Continue until 30 players make
> the cut, and take an additional 0 to 4 players (the top-scoring
> no-GW-getting players) as needed to make day 2 a multiple of five. This
> has the daunting problem of determining seating, since seating cannot
> be made until a round is entirely over, and would have to be done by
> hand.

This idea I really like :) May I propose a model?

Round 1:
Standard format applies for round 1 of competition

Round 2:
All players who achieve a GW in round 1 are removed from the tournament
as LSJ preposes. You now have "X" players avaliable to do other things.
One option is (and I have no idea if it is viable or not) is that these
X players playtest the up and coming yearly storyline event decks/cards
while round 2 is going on. Not only would this provide some useful
player feedback for WW, but who would not give their left inscisor to
help shape a game that they love to play?
If this option is unavailiable, then the first qualifiers could play
for a "bounty" similar to the ones offered this year at the NAC.

Additionally there could also be a "bonus VP" offered to the player
who wins, added to thier standing for the next days competition. This
way even if a player qualifies there is a real incentive to keep
playing to win rather than resting on thier laurels.

Round 3
Once again the players who achive a GW in round 2 are added to the list
of qualifiers for day 2 and are removed from further competition. This
group of "Y" players is merged with the "X" players to play a "sudden
death" single round event where the winner takes all, all being a
"bounty" and an additional VP to take with them to day 2, once more
pushing the play to win aspect of the game.

Day 2
Day 2 occours as it does now except those that qualifed early have a
potential edge in standings from their previously accrued VP's (much
like option 2)

>
> 4) Make a single 5+F tournament, spread over 2 days. Again a bit of a
> seating problem creeps in. And the kingmaking aspect of being
> eliminated from the finals before round 5 begins. Plus the unfun aspect
> of playing the same deck five times in a row.

5 rounds in one continuous event IMHO only favours the "cheesemonkies"
and the "table dealers", not exactly the PTW theory as I understand it.
In theory it could work, but I can't really trust that theory, too many
time outs, table splits and mutual withdrawals prevail in my Vtes
world. If you want to play in a hardcore tournament, play to win or as
Ankur says:
Play. the. game.

Sutekh_23

I thought that seeding players after the first round would work nicely
to give them incentive to play for those GWs. I just now worked out how
to modify the Archon first round (top 25 players) so that this
advantage works. Here ya go, but it's messy.

The first set of three rows are the three rounds of the tournament,
with players numbered from 1 to 25 according to their rank after the
first day of the tournament.

For reference, the second set of three rows are the "strength of
schedule" for each of the players listed above where those are
arithmetic averages of their opponents for every round.

The first seed has a strength of schedule of 16.00 for each of the
three rounds. This means the first seed's average opponent for every
game is 16th seed.

Each successive seed has a more difficult strength of schedule by 0.25,
with the 25th seed having a strength of schedule of 10.00 (average
opponent is 10th seed). It turns out with this particular setup that
each player has the exact same SoS for each of the three games. It also
happens that influence order is preserved and no pairings are
duplicated (identical to the original in the Archon).

I figured this out by brute force here with a spreadsheet, but there
*must* be some elegant algorithm underlying which can allow the Archon
to seed 30, 35, etc size events.

Enjoy.

Jeff

The thing about that is, the influence of luck is only reduced in the long
run. Even six or seven trials isn't that much the long run, here. Luck
could still result in plenty of feast-or-famine decks being played and
making finals.

Some form of Swiss seating for a 5+F or 6+F two-day event might be
interesting (at least on paper) - I'm not sure if people would really be
excited by playing the same deck six or seven times in a row, but if you
played against other players with the same number of GWs as you, you could
mostly avoid the problem of facing players with nothing to do but kingmake.

multi-deck - change to a different deck for every game if you want. That
could (a) eliminate the advantage of scouting and (b) keep the players
interested in playing their various decks. Though it is a problem if we
want to crown a deck as well as a player as the "Continental Champion". And
it might require players to have quite a few strong decks built and
available if they want to take advantage of variety while still playing
winning decks.

Josh

Whatever solution is used needs to be simple for judges to implement
and also easy for players to understand:

e.g.:
Day 1
Play first 3 rounds with 1 constructed legal deck - top 40% of players
go through to day 2

Day 2
You may play the same deck or another deck that is constructed legal as
day 1.
Only points earned on day 2 count towards final standing.
Top 5 players from day 2 go through to final as normal

I'd be quite happy to see any easily udnerstood and easy to implement
system be used for the NAC and other large events.
E.g. 3r each day counting towards total results or 5r &f.
Anything with players dropping between rounds seems foolish and makes a
mockery of the 'removing too much luck aspect' from the game e.g. if
you had a really lucky first table but your deck and your style
probably would have not got you any further in the day 1 ratings than
those points.

I would agree that there was a definate lacklustre affair to some of
the games day 1 and I certianly recall switching off a little as the
day went on (after my first round GW), an environment where every GW
and VP was important on day 1 may encourage more PTW.

> > I couldn't say, but I suppose that in the vast majority of cases, it

Yes, it's legal. It's not just your pure chances of winning, it's the

analysis. I know there are many previous threads on play-to-win, but
the following thread is one of the best:

Messages.Author: ira...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
First, I think it's important to note and appreciate the willingness of
our head tournament organizer to solicit feedback from the playerbase.
I do not take this for granted, and it's one of the major things that
makes this game as fun as it is. Thank you, LSJ!

> 1) Don't make 40 the fixed cutoff line. Take only 25 or 30 or 35,
> depending on the participation level.

As discussed elsewhere in this thread, I think this option is best. It
creates a greater incentive to go for the GW, because a higher
threshold is required. Once players realize they need at least a GW to
make it to the next day, players will be going for the GW.

> 2) Count GWs on day 1 as additional VPs on day 2 (making every GW
> important again). That is, a player with 2GWs and 9VPs on day 1 and 1GW
> and 4VPs on day 2 is counted as 1GW 6VPs for purposes of getting into
> the finals of day 2.

I like the idea that I start with a clean slate on day 2, but I also
like the idea that day 1 makes a difference. :) I think we should
first try raising the bar to make it to day 2 per suggestion #1, and if
that's not enough, then also add this.

> 3) Day 1 is an unsanctioned elimination tournament, but in reverse.
> After the first round, all players with game wins qualify for day 2 and
> are removed from the remainder of day 1. Continue until 30 players make
> the cut, and take an additional 0 to 4 players (the top-scoring
> no-GW-getting players) as needed to make day 2 a multiple of five. This
> has the daunting problem of determining seating, since seating cannot
> be made until a round is entirely over, and would have to be done by
> hand.

I definitely don't like this one, because it's very complicated,
significantly different from different tournament structures, and is
less fun for people who win early.

> 4) Make a single 5+F tournament, spread over 2 days. Again a bit of a
> seating problem creeps in. And the kingmaking aspect of being
> eliminated from the finals before round 5 begins. Plus the unfun aspect
> of playing the same deck five times in a row.

You could get around the problem of the same deck by letting people
vary decks, but even so I don't like this one for the reasons you
mentioned. It's no fun to be in round 5 without any hope of making the
finals.

Thanks again for listening. I think the subtle change of raising the
bar for day 2 will make enough of a difference to encourage a greater
desire for GWs.

Ira

low metric, 1 VPs, then only decks that can't score a VP are

choose to act this way, are going to figure out the performance
required and then shoot for that.

In defense of LSJ, and of the players in general, I saw a lot of dealing for
2 VP in day 1, but I think that most of it was reasonable under the rules.
Even when I was on the short end of the deal, I never felt it was necessary
to call for a ruling from Scott. I would rather there were more looking
left, as opposed to looking cross-table, but I don't think the x-table
looking that occurred was illegal.

I had a nice talk with Christian Chenard during the late-night pick-up
session after day 2, and he felt that it was more of a stylistic difference
with certain playgroups. I'm clearly paraphrasing his comments, so any
misunderstanding is on me, but it seems that his playgroup is quicker to
accept the 3-2 split, if they feel it is highly likely to shake out that
way, even if it is early in the game. E.g., if Player A feels his chances of
earning 2 VP in a deal to give Player B 3 VP are about 50 or 60%, vs a 5 or
10% chance of getting the GW himself, then he'll deal for the 2 as soon as
possible. (The example is mine, but I think it gets the point across.)

This tendency in his playgroup may explain why he was willing to accept a
3-2 (his GW) split from me in day 2, round 3, even though he suspected I
would break the deal. (Since neither Norm nor Adam was willing to deal with
him at all.) As it turned out, he couldn't quite close out Adam by himself,
and I did break the deal and make my way into the final thanks to those 4
VP.

- Pat

P.S. On an unrelated note, since I haven't gotten around to posting a WoN
report, I would like to say that it was a huge pleasure to game with so many
new players during the Week... Christian, TX gang, LA crew, Seattlites, Euro
visitors, plus many of the usual suspects that I've met before. Thanks for a
great event, everyone.

P.P.S. I had not definitely decided to break the deal until the turn before
I ousted... but when Christian was on 2 pool with no Tupdog in play, I had
to go for it.

I think the only way to really solve the issue of players
"prequalifying" by getting one (or even 2) game wins early and then
being able to shrug off round two or three is by making Game Wins on
day 1 count for something besides just moving on to day 2.

The reward shouldn't be so great that it overly rewards feast-or-famine
play, but gaining the bonus VP, bonus pool/transfers, or even
strength-of-schedule rewards mentioned in this thread would be worth
considering.

Alternatively, every player that makes it to the finals of day 2 starts
with an extra pool for each game win on day 1 and 2 combined. This
makes the day 1 GWs only especially meaningful if you also do well on
day 2, but doesn't doubly-reward feast-or-famine decks (i.e., they have
to get lucky both days in order to gain a larger advantage over any
other deck type, whereas under the other proposals getting lucky day 1
gives you an advantage in all your games day 2, making it easier to get
"lucky" again).

day 2.

Yeah, I can recognize the ideal. To elaborate on the problem, though; once
a table starts to deal to split the table, if you remain apart from those
conversations, you are putting yourself in a position that is likely to
lose. Since this is an international event, groups more prone towards
table deals, and who don't take issue with it, can alter the table dynamic
significantly, even in small numbers. Our (Josh D. and My) table one had
its table splitting negotaitions started by Andreas. It didn't reach the
conclusion he'd hoped for, but that's beside the point. My table three was
first negotiated to a split by Christian Chenard. Had I not finally moved
away at that point from a prior position of choosing to not participate in
negotiations, I would not have gotten even the 2 VP from that table.

This is not a negative commentary on either Andreas or Christian, of
course. For them, negotiating a table they cannot hope to win by
themselves _is_ playing. the. game. Once two people at a table head down
that road, the rest invariably must participate (even if only to ally
themselves against the dealmakers). Entreating people to Play The Game
doesn't address this issue _nearly_ sufficiently enough.

DaveZ

Depends on how you define dealbreaking. Day 1 Round 3, my prey had
ousted his prey and by that time I had built up quiet a large Ravnos
Laibon army and was starting to go after my prey. My grandprey had the
option to block my prey (his predator) and really mess him up in
combat. He was concerned about how easy a free ride I would get out of
it. We agreed that if he did, I would let him get his prey before I
would oust him. I was able to make short work of my prey, since this
deal let me put Week of Nightmares into play with one less player that
would move Week counters (wasn't part of the deal, but we were buddies
now) and that also helped him because he was playing Anarch Ravnos.
After getting my prey, I saw back a couple turns, waiting for him to
oust his prey. His prey was able to bounce his bleeds, I think had a
Blood Doll for some pool gain, and got rid of his Army of Rats. Time
was starting to tick down, so I decided that my new prey was unable to
keep his end of the deal (ousting his prey), so I decided to oust him.
Did I break my deal? Probably, but maybe not. Depends on how you view
deals. Either way, I ended with my GW and made it to Day 2, so I'd do
it again.

> no-GW-getting players) as needed to make day 2 a multiple of five. This
> has the daunting problem of determining seating, since seating cannot
> be made until a round is entirely over, and would have to be done by
> hand.

This option makes a GW worth the most relative to a VP. In fact, if
you were to skip taking the addition 0 to 4 players with no GWs, it
would make VPs completely worthless. Making VPs worthless would be a
surefire way to eliminate the gray area between playing for GWs and
playing for VPs.

The seating problem could be overcome through the use of a spreadsheet
or a webpage/webapp that was created specifically to handle the issue.

True, but not especially enlightening.

Compare with the V:EKN-wide rules change that was initiated when VPs
were made secondary to Game Wins/Table Wins. That the previous
structure, with the difference between 3VP and 2VP being so minimal that
table splits were extremely easy to convince people to take and a number
of consistent problems with (for example) annoying intercept decks that
*only* played for last-man standing to get 6VP over the course of a
tournament (quite possibly enough to reach the finals in a small
tournament), was unacceptable to many people was also a matter that was
totally subjective:

>The rules set the baseline for behavior at the NAC. The rules are
>agreed upon by all the participants.

And those were the rules that everyone was playing to. You couldn't
blame the people making the many, many table-slicing deals because they
were playing to the best advantage given the table at the time, and the
rules structure at the time. That was precisely the point. They were
doing things that were good for them (at least as they understood it -
but a judge cannot step in to correct bad play, or improve play based on
a fuller knowledge of game state). You can't get a judge to step in and
say "This play is distasteful and so you cannot do it." That way,
madness lies.

And in the situation of people not playing to win, it is extremely hard
to intervene because it's not necessarily an open and obvious thing.
They want to qualify, more than anything else, so they play to qualify.
This can involve many subtle and non-obvious, and even non-conscious,
decisions by a player. Do they go for broke and sweep-or-bust, or do
they play for a more subtle 2VPs on this table, because it will solidify
their rank and put them solidly inside the top 40? Will you be able to
tell after 10 goes round the table whether or not a potential oust on
turn 5 was or wasn't taken because they didn't have the cards in hand,
or because they were worried about other considerations? Enforcing play
to win is fine when there's a deal to be made - it's much harder when a
player has changed their own perception of what's important, based on
the rules.

Thus, change the targets that are important to them, meaning that they
have to play-to-win in order to reliably progress - rather than play to
draw, or play to come a respectable second giving them an outcome
they're happy with.

Changing the tournament rules from VPs to GWs absolutely, fundamentally
altered the targets players needed to aim for. First and foremost, they
need GWs. 2VP is not anywhere near as good as 3VP on a table split
(except on a 2-1-1-1-0 split). This changed player behaviour. There
are a lot fewer poor intercept decks that don't intend to go forward,
because 0GWs and 6 VP is a *much* poorer performance than even 1GW and
3VP.

Subjectively, those creating the rules - and those discussing the rules
at the time - didn't like some of the behaviour that the existing rules
structure encouraged. That people at the time were playing to the rules
was not the point - all power to the people who do well under whatever
set of rules. However, if the rules lead to some subjective problems
that are subjectively disliked by players, it is worth considering a
change.

The best form of change is change that leads to players enforcing the
new standards for themselves, because it is in their interests to do so.
Want players to play for table wins? Then make them important. Want
players to play for sweeps? Then rank sweeps above all else.

>I have not heard of one person who had a "Bad" time at the NAC. I have
>heard of a bunch of players, who from impressions gathered are not in
>"Dealmaking" playgroups. When they get to the NAC and see the players
>from "Dealmaking" playgroup make a bunch of deals on the table while
>they are caught flatfooted, then they complain that a multi-player game
>isn't supposed to have dealmaking, which is ludicrous on its face.

I didn't hear many people telling me how bad a time they'd had at a
tournament I was at under the VP-only system, whether I was playing or
judging. Lots of people enjoyed playing V:TES in a friendly but
competitive environment with people they didn't see that often, come
what may. They may have found a particular table annoying, but they
didn't go away telling everyone how bad a time they'd had.

If, then, we need a non-subjective change, players must have been
playing under some other rules structure that wasn't agreed to by them,
and we need players to be openly telling us how bad a time they have at
tournaments before a rules change can be made... when will you be
campaigning to a return to the VP only system?

That was a subjective change made to a system that all players had
agreed to play under, and some people found the effects annoying but
weren't telling everyone how bad a time they had at major tournaments,
so it is clearly an entirely illegitimate rules change. By the
standards you are expressing here, that is.

If the GW rules are fine, however, what's the difference here? Players
play under the rules, some players don't like some of the effects (but
enjoy the tournaments nevertheless), players discuss rules change.
Which is, in fact, exactly the same procedure as for pretty much every
other rules change that's ever been made by V:EKN and every card
banning:

1) People happy to play but would prefer a change that they believe
would make games more open, competitive and fun (e.g. tweaks to the
multi-action rules so that some decks are much less affected, or the
banning of Succubus Club)
->
2) idea considered by appropriate people (V:EKN, Rules Team, rules-
writers/Design Team, or whoever is appropriate for that particular
change)
->
3) idea implemented or rejected, based on the subjective merits of the
arguments put forward, and the subjective evaluation of player behaviour
seen by the relevant people.

You appear to be arguing that this rules change suggestion must pass a
whole mountain of criteria that have never been applied in the past,
before even being discussed.

Why?

goal of achieving a GW over merely a few VPs.

Agreed; that was my understanding as well, albeit with the caveat that
we're talking about "not just decktypes that can get 2-3 GWs" in three
preliminary round games - as opposed to five or six preliminary round
games. (So, for instance, LSJ's option #4 still satisfies this point,
as do all of his options IMHO.) The point, I believe, has to do with not
biasing the tournament towards high-risk, high-reward type decks and thus
having a tournament whose character was at odds with what people are used
to in, say, a CQ tournament. Or at least, I'm assuming this last part
but I think it's fairly accurate description of the reasoning.

> The current model satifies that goal. Now we have a
> new goal which is to keep players from trying to take advantage of that
> model. In the next year or two it will change to restructure it again.

Agreed the current model satisfies that goal. But it has another problem.
If we satisfy one goal with a tournament structure change, must we ignore
all other new issues that we discover along the way?

Yes, if we solve this new problem and find yet a third distinct problem
in our next choice, then I suppose you would be right: we would restructure
it yet again in a year or two. I don't see how that's a given, however.
And if it happens, I don't really see it as bad problem. Sometimes things
like this take a while to get right. But you'll never get a thing right
if you ignore the problems.

>> I will repeat: the first day format would appear to emphasize the need to
>> rack up victory points rather than game wins. Therefore, the "elegance of
>> that (the game win) fix" in the current first day has been bypassed. All
>> of LSJ's suggestion are geared towards addressing that point.
>
> The first day format emphasises getting to the second day. With 65
> players, that gives us an availible pool of 39 Game Wins which is
> almost exactly the number of second day spots So why were there so few
> game wins? The answer is because players won't "Shut Up and Play the
> Game".

And the reason people won't "shut up and play the game"? Isn't is possible
that the perceived need to just score a high number of victory points,
rather than get game wins, is exactly _why_ all the negotiation? It
seems logical to me that people planning decks to take victory points and
split tables is, in part, a self-fulfilling prophesy. I also think
expecting 39 tables to provide 39 game wins to 39 separate players in a
tournament is outrageously naive. Under the best of circumstances there
probably wouldn't be more than 30 and I suspect more than 25 is probably
a better estimate.

Whatever the reason, some people apparently perceived game wins were
unnecessary on the first day and: 1) that perception proved to be accurate;
and also 2) that perception automatically causes the same problem which
is why the game win was invented. The answer is the same: fix the
tournament structure so you don't need to run your judges around to all
the tables to MAKE PEOPLE "shut up and play the game" - nor (worse!) have
to make lots of hairy judgements about when they should give that order.

> The problem isn't the number of spots in the second day. The problem
> is the players.

Since the problem can be solved by altering the format, it seems much
better to do that. Solving it by injecting copious amounts of judicial
fiat is not going to be most peoples' choice, IME. And, again - this
is the exact same thinking that was why we went to the game win in the
first place: giving players the right incentive to play to win is better
than making judges render subjective determinations about when they are
or are not doing that.

I kind of get the impression we haven't really heard your real reason
for resisting a change. I don't think it's just that another change to
the format is too soon. OK, you like the existing format. But what
is it about the existing format that you would miss under all the
proposals to change it?

Fred

My game 2 went to time primarily because there were three intercept

I'm on the fence as to whether there is actually a problem or not. I
did hear people state/suggest that they were just playing to move onto
day 2, but I did not actually witness any play that suggested that was
true.

I do not however think that it is known that the 'problem' can be fixed
by changing the format. I would simply suggest that if people feel
there is any illegal dealing going on at their table that they should
call the judge. I think that people are simply unwilling to call for a
judge in most circumstances and that is the 'problem' if one indeed
exists. I have judged a large number of tournaments in my time as
prince of Denver, CO and Washington D.C. I do not think that I was
asked for a ruling on anything more than 10 times in the 10 years I was
a tournament organizer. I am the same way...I don't want to bother the
judge especially if it gives the perception that I do not trust my
fellow players.

I am personally not opposed to change, however I do not think we need
to change the NAC format because of a problem that may not be all that
bad (not seen among the players I played with on day one; 20% of the
player pool, only 8% of tables, however, so those players could have
been involved in table split deals at other tables).

Then again I will add my two cents to what changes I would
suggest...not to the NAC format, but to the tournament rules...for all
tournaments:

******************************************
All deals that involve VPs should be presided over by a judge to make a
ruling on legality, and time should stop during the negotiation.
*******************************************

This would lengthen some games, at least initially, but would probably
also result in fewer timeouts in these games.
I also think it would reduce the dealing for VPs, especially early game
deals, and table splits would decrease in turn.

jon

While I think illegal dealling is certainly something that folks are
concerned about, the current format also has the problem of (at least
in theory) encouraging people to play incredibly defensive decks that
are of the "I'm incapable of getting a game win, but boy can I get
2VP!" type. Which are bad for the game in a general sense (not that
they exist, but it is bad for the game that people are inordinately
encouraged to play such decks)--the current 2 day format rewards
incredibly defensive decks and rewards getting 2VPs consistiently over
game wins inconsistiently. Which is certainly something that would be
good to fix.

> I think that people are simply unwilling to call for a
> judge in most circumstances and that is the 'problem' if one indeed exists.

While certainly a reasonable statement, games usually work better when
they are designed to circumvent the need to call a judge in the first
place. Yeah, you can just say "If something bad happens, call the
judge!", but as it is human nature to not so much do this (especially
in what is essentially a friendly, light hearted social game), it is
likely better to structure the event to minimize the need for this sort
of activity.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Jon wrote:
> I'm not sure I understand your point, Peter. I would not want to
> discourage people from playing defensive decks well.

To be fair, I wasn't at the NAC, so this is all theoretical, based on
the discussion that followed. But from what I'm seeing, the current two
day format of the NAC means that on the first day, you don't need to
worry about actually winning games; you just need to get a couple VPs
per game and can safely ignore GWs (so as to get enough VPs to safely
be in the top X players to advance to the next day). This means that
folks who want to play the system are strongly encouraged to show up
with decks that can reliably get 2VPs per game but aren't necessarily
capable of winning games (see: incredibly defensive wall decks that get
2VPs by being the last guy standing). If enough people come into day 1
with this mind set ("I don't need to win, I just need to get 2 VPs per
game..."), the environment is kind of wonky, and people stop "playing
to win" and instead are "playing to get 2VPs", which is not how that
game is supposed to work. The second day is likely all about game wins
(which is good). But the first day (which is the issue at hand) seems
to reward not playing to win.

> People can and will play bad decks/fun decks/whatever because they want
> to and this should not be discouraged as long as they are trying to win
> while playing bad/fun/goofy decks. It is the trying to win part that is
> potentially in need of fixing not the decks played.

I'm talking about the built in incentive--I'm not suggesting that
people should be specifically discouraged from playing certain deck
types. I'm suggesting that the format of the event should be adjusted
to reward playing decks that can win games rather than reward decks
that are incredibly defensive and get 2VPs--the current format rewards
decks that can't win but can get 2VPs (in a 5 player game), as about
2VPs per game is all you need to advance.

> I do agree that calling a judge should be circumvented if possible, but
> there are situations in this game which I think demands it - i.e. the
> VP deal.

Oh, sure--I totally agree and realize that sometimes it is necessary.
But again, like the above situation I'm talking about, if the structure
of the event was adjusted to *not* reward or encourage playing for 2VPs
(as opposed to a GW), people will be less likely to accept the 2 side
of a 2/3 split, let alone go looking for one.

The current system for day one (Top X players of day 1 advance, and you
get to be in the Top X by virtue of having, say, 6VP over 3 games)
rewards both defensive play and defensive decks (as opposed to
agressive play and agressive decks) and finding a justification to
accepting the short end of a 3/2 split deal.

-Peter

I think the point is, this part of this tournament shouldn't encourage
OR discourage any particular type of deck in relation to each other.
But unfortutely, tournament structures can't avoid having some effect
in terms of dictating the character of decks played. So what's
considered "good" should be a structure that avoids unfun play and
decks that lead to unfun play. That accomplished, the tournament
structure at a continental championship should be consistent with
the other levels of play. This was the essential reasoning (in my
estimation) for making the change to a two-day championship in the
first place: that the one-day format encouraged a different type
of deck than a one-day format encompassing the kinds of numbers that
would play at continental qualifier. By the same token, a day in which
success is defined by acquiring two victory points and no game wins in
three games doesn't fill the bill either. So it's not a matter
of figuring out that the format encourages or discourages some
particular type of deck and editing the rules based on that as much
as it is simply noting that has an effect on how people plan
strategy and thus build decks and how they play decks.

Fred

That doesn't mean that no compromise can be reached. I have no problem
at all with 2.5 VPs getting you to day 2. That's at least holding your
own against many of the best VtES players in the world. But it's not
unreasonable to let people who place higher on day 1 carry at least
some advantage into day 2. The trick is finding a medium between overly
rewarding the "feast-or-famine" decks and overly rewarding the "just
need 1 VP every game" decks.

thinks he needs just 1 or 2 more VPs to sneak into day 2 looking for or
accepting a deal that guarantees those VP. But we may be able do

> through the tournament that it will turn into a 25 percent chance is
> well, frankly, an idiot.

Risk analysis isn't a strategy in and of itself. It's an activity. The
assumed strategy coupled with risk analysis is that you'll choose the path
with least risk. You're appealing to such a path. However, the point is
that the increased risk of choosing a progressively less optimal path may
not be enough of a deterrent to a player to sufficiently dissuade them
from making such a choice, since they are not making such a decision in a
vaccuum. Considerations such as deck type, comfort level, entertainment,
and desire to play with "Elihu" also factor in, and may have a more
critical role in the deck selection process. Since deck variety increases
as a person relaxes their scale of "viable decks" (in accordance with said
risk analysis), it becomes suddenly possible to consider a situation where
a person does not *need* to play for the GW, again, according to some
non-optimal risk analysis.

Now, let's muck up all that theoretical shit.

If everyone chooses an optimal path (i.e. play for the GW), it's *still*
not clear that there will be fewer non-GW slots to day 2, since one of
your conditions (namely, the one that a person scores more than 1 GW)
coincides with the goal of earning more GWs. Moreover, timeouts are still
possible, even if everyone is choosing to play for GWs. These facts allows
for the bottom-feeding VP whore to exist and thrive even in *this* kind of
an environment.

As far as risk analysis, I would bet that with a 40/65 ratio, at least 10
tables over the day would time out or grant a GW to someone who already
has one. I'd put the chance of that happening at 80% or more, given past
experience. That's a pretty fair percentage in general, even though it's
manufactured. Following along with that, there would then be 11 non-GW
slots that would advance to day 2. A bottom-feeder has a roughly 1/6
chance of advancing to day 2 if he goes along with his strategy.

As a final note, I'd like to point out that there are a great number of
decks that can manage VPs and resist ousting without having really any
hope of a GW. Dependable intercepty decks with short chain combat, and
decks that protect pool with dominate and votes or obf/aus are among this
camp. Well, maybe not dominate. Dominate has this nasty habit of actually
winning games.

To find a massive collection of wildly ineffective decks that resemble
small woodland animals having an orgasm in the rain moments before being

offerings. . . the flagship deck being, of course Elihu with a meathook. A
key component of this deck is to also go anarch and then pay a pool to
rush with Elihu each turn with inferior combat based on melee weapons and
little means to protect pool.

> Big Fan of Ankur "Super-Smart" Gupta

No. This causes potential issues with 5.2 of the V:EKN rules:

Players must not play toward goals that conflict with the goal
of the game as stated in the V:TES rulebook (e.g., attacking
certain players on the basis of their V:EKN ratings or overall
tournament standing, etc.).

If the play-to-win situation that a player would be inclined to take
(either as the recipient of the GW or maximising VPs due to a crappy
situation) under ordinary circumstances is a VP-split deal, and they
chose not to take it because it would ruin their entry to another
tournament, they would be playing towards a goal that conflicted with
the goal of the game.

No player, of course, is required to take a deal (because they think
someone is lying, for example), but you don't really want cases where a
player isn't playing as competitively as they would choose to because of
an external inducement.

they're making little enough headway into their prey that it's their
best chance at a(nother) VP, and sometimes their predator allows it
because the withdrawing player has enough pool and/or permanents to
defend it that allowing that player to leave the table gives the
predator a better shot at VPs. If you make withdrawing worth only as

Messages.Author: ira...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:
> So how's this for a fix (applied only to VEKN tournaments -- leaving
> the basic gamne rules alone): award just 0.5 VPs for a withdrawal
> rather than the full VP. "Last Methuselah Standing" would still get a
> full VP, making "mutual withdrawal" not quite the same as going to
> time.
>
> Either that or eliminate withdrawal (and ban Brinksmanship), like ante
> was eliminated for tournaments back in 1995.

I like that you're considering this as a possibility, and also
soliciting feedback. Thank you!

I like the possibility of Brinksmanship. I'm confident there would be
a way to keep it in the game, regardless of what change you make to
withdrawl.

It seems like the ways withdrawl occurs in practice is:
1) 3-2 table split
2) 4-1 or 3-1 pity VP ("you were a good wall") after someone already
has the GW
3) Actual withdrawl

It seems like everyone agrees that #3 is very rare, and no one seems
heartbroken about losing it for the greater good.

#1 is the thing that we want to disincentivize. Say we have a table
A->B->C->D->E. A has a strong vote deck; D also has a vote deck, but
isn't doing as well. Instead of fighting it out, D agrees to the
losing end of a 3-2 table split.

If withdrawl was disallowed, this deal couldn't happen because once it
got down to A->D, A nor D wouldn't have a way of getting just 1 more
VP. If withdrawl was allowed, but only worth 0.5 VPs, this deal still
works fine, because A could withdraw for 2.5 VPs, and D ends with 2
VPs, still giving the GW to A. In fact, if we use the 0.5 withdraw
rules, it might make the table split even more appealing to D, because
it's only a 0.5 VP difference.

Assuming withdrawl isn't possible, the deal could still happen just
fine if A was dealing with B, C, or E, since withdrawl isn't used in
those cases.

So it seems to me that removing withdrawl entirely really only stops
the 3-2 split with your grand-predator, and if you allow a 0.5
withdrawl, that doesn't stop the 3-2 splits at all (and it might make
them more desirable.)

For #2 above, the 3-1 or 4-1 pity VP, I actually like that it's
possible. It gives someone in a losing situation something to hope
for. Hope is important, and makes the game fun. It also encourages
them to stay in the game, and not simply self-oust out of hopelessness.

Consider the table A->B->C->D->E, where A is very strong, and E has no
hope of ousting A. I've seen (been in) this situation many times. A
offers to E, "If you stay alive until the end of the game, I'll let you
withdraw." Somewhere along the line, maybe C or D gets ousted, but A
is the strongest deck, E hangs on, and A gets 2 or 3 VPs. The endgame
A->E, normally A would allow E to withdraw, but if withdrawl was
illegal, then A and E would have to agree to a draw, giving E a measley
0.5 VP.

Therefore, removing withdrawl doesn't really stop the pity VP for
staying alive, but it does make it less appealing. That would have the
effect of making E more likely to suicide himself into A, and/or just
ousting himself outright.

Personally, I'd rather that people who can't oust their prey have
something else to hope for, instead of just self-ousting. Removing the
withdrawl rule reduces their hope from 1VP to 0.5 VP, which seems too
small to me.

I'm sure there are other cases, but I feel like the above situations
cover a lot of the cases.

In conclusion, my initial reaction was that removing the withdrawl
rules would do a lot of good, and help stop table split deals. After
looking at the deals that would actually be stopped, I don't think
removing withdrawl actually helps that much, and it does hurt in some
ways.

I think the best solution is to change the tournament structure
(especially at big tournaments) to more strongly encourage game wins
over VPs.

Thanks for asking and listening,
Ira

Debating whether or not the VP deals are a good thing (TM) might be

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Nov 29, 9:41 pm, "Rob Grau" <rfg...@eos.ncsu.edu> wrote:
> I didn't see an arguement that the withdrawal rule itself was abusive,
> and given that I'd like it to stay in the [tourney] game.

It is certainly arguable that the Withdrawl rule, which exists
originally to provide last ditch incentive for forward momentum in
stalemate games (i.e. if the game is at a lock, and no one is willing
to move, someone can attempt to withdraw, compelling his predator to
take action), is, in fact, being abused in that it is, in practice,
only used to facilitate deal making (which is not likely the inetent of
the rule in the first place) in that "How about I let you live, you
oust your prey and then withdraw, and I walk away with 3VP" kinda way.
As the withdrawl rule is rarely, if ever, used for its actual intended
purpose (to force action in a stalemate) due to there being a timelimit
in tournament play, the vast, vast majority of the uses of the
withdrawl rule in competetive play could arguably be called "abusive".

I don't think that the game would suffer at all if withdrawing was
removed from competetive play (removing one more bargaining chip from
the arsenal of folks who like to wheel and deal rather than oust their
prey), and the collaterall damage of killing Brinksmanship could be
fixed rather easily by making a very similar card that did not require
the withdrawing mechanism.

-Peter

The thing of it is, eliminating the withdrawal rule completely doesn't
really stop VP deals anyway, it just alters the amount that can be
offered depending on seating. You can still make winning or losing 3/2
deals with your predator or prey. You can make a losing 3/2 deal with
your grandpredator, and a winning 3/2 deal with your grandprey. I'm not
so sure that eliminating the withdrawal rule will actually help all
that much, and I'm especially concerned that it seems likely to reduce
cross-table deals more than neighbor deals.

I mean, I don't know about anyone else, but I'm a lot more frustrated
when someone makes a deal with their prey than I am when two guys
crosstable make a pact - at least the crosstable deal was made in
keeping with the initial predator/prey relationship.

Crosstable deals are also often ways of getting VPs _now_ instead of
pushing the game out to a time limit. I'd still much rather people make
shorter-term deals (like, I'll help you get 1VP, you help me get 1VP,
then we see where the table stands before talking about anything more
than that), but that just doesn't seem to happen so much.

Withdraw deals occur with great frequency and almost always result in

What I find the most interesting about this proposal is that it would
still allow players to mutually withdraw at the two-player level,
provided such was still play-to-win for both of them (i.e, time is
running out or the player in the stronger position wins by agreeing to
the withdrawal - and is in a sufficiently stronger position that the
other player is justified in accepting 1 VP instead trying to play for
2).

This could make it difficult in some situations to determine if the
players are making decisions solely on game state if they had a prior
deal. That doesn't make this a bad idea, as it would certainly change
the outcome of at least some deals, and I would think that most games
would still need to be played out. If it turned out that players began
abusing this "loophole" you could modify play-to-win by stating that in
the two-player game, each player must play to maximize VPs regardless
of the game win (i.e., they could only withdraw if there was a
stalemate).

> This seems to be the way it should always have been and it seemingly

Who is that guy anyway? Let's beat the crap out of him.

> significant debates that has appeared on the newsgroup for a long time
> and could significantly change the face of the game. More opinions and

My concern is that it may be difficult to adjudicate the proposed "game
state only" endgame in practice. Neither of the two players involved would
call a judge to make sure the parameters are met (since it's in their best
interest *not* to do so), and everyone else is a spectator (and thus, may
not be allowed to watch the game). Unless there's a judge present at
*every* table who watches the game until it finishes from a two-player
state, I hardly see the proposed solution as actually being a solution.

Moreover, it's already difficult for a judge to distinguish between dumb
play and play with an ulterior motive (upholding a prior deal that isn't
necessarily privy to a judge). I couldn't even begin to imagine what kind
of a nightmare that would be for judges. ("Oops, I accidentally called
this KRC when I was on 1 pool and passed it. Shucks.") In the end, there's
an underlying ethic about playing the game. My calling card is thought of
as a bit tongue-in-cheek here (and it is), but really, it captures a whole
host of issues.

Play. The. Game.

It's that easy.

To that end, we are attempting to apply a series of changes so that the
game ethic matches reality. I feel that a change to the reward for
withdrawing would be a positive first step. Remove the reward (1 VP), or
have simply add some tournament points for a successful withdrawal. That
will help. However, I've argued that it may *yet* not solve the problem --
it may simply skew 3/2 deals in favor of certain relationships on a 5
player table. It should be tested.

Ankur
Play. The. Game.

On Dec 1, 4:06 am, Ankur Gupta <agu...@cs.duke.edu> wrote:
> Moreover, it's already difficult for a judge to distinguish between dumb

> this KRC when I was on 1 pool and passed it. Shucks.") In the end, there's
> an underlying ethic about playing the game. My calling card is thought of
> as a bit tongue-in-cheek here (and it is), but really, it captures a whole
> host of issues.

Yeah, see, this is why I am vastly more in favor of concrete, objective
tweaks to the rules (i.e. removal of the Withdrawl rule, at least in
tournaments, where it isn't needed for its intended purpose anyway)
than subjective tweaks that require *more* judgement from judges (i.e.
adjusting what is or is not a legal deal in the game).

While removal of the Withdrawl rule might not fix everything that needs
fixing, it is at least simple and non subjective and probably would go
a ways towards eliminating a lot of silly deals due to lack of
incentive. Mucking around with "this deal is legal, but this deal
isn't" kinda stuff can't, in theory, hurt anything, but strikes me as
less likely to actually accomplish anything, for reasons pointed out by
Ankur.

-Peter

Yes, I owe James an apology for being short with him.

These are the avenues I'm thinking about towards solving your (Ira's?)
challenge for a different tournament structure--

1. Emphasize GWs over VPs by not counting VPs at all. This would leave
us in a tiebreak bind because even tournament points have a basis in
VPs. I haven't thought of a tiebreak solution that didn't use VPs in
some way.

2. Using some sort of ladder format for tournaments. This quickly
gets complicated with V:TES' multiplayer games. Maybe workable, but I
haven't figured out how.

3. Since people are concerned about table spilts, some mechanic to
encourage earning VPs. This is opposed to Ira's notion of
deemphasizing VPs, which is a problem. (and where I got tripped up
earlier) Also at issue is that VPs themselves are probably the best
way of doing this. the simplest, at least.

4. Seeding a tournament based on V:EKN ranking, followed by a knockout
elimination instead of prelim rounds. Since every game does not have a
GW, this would need some adjusting to make work.

It's also possible that none of these ideas will actually turn out
better than our current tournament stucture.

Perhaps someone can improve on one of the things I was considering.

Rob Grau
rfg...@eos.ncsu.edu

Messages.Author: Clément
Messages.Body:
LSJ escreveu:

> Perhaps (in addition or in place of a change to withdrawal rules), "Play to win"
> could be revisited to demand that self-preservation override any deals. That is,
> any "and I'll let you oust me" or "and I'll self-oust" deals would be disallowed
> (forcing their ilk into strangely-couched verbal contortions that hopefully can
> be sniffed out).

I like this idea. However, I wonder how would us judges be able to
enforce "self-preservation".

A lot of times I have seem players justify questionable decisions based
on them being in a lost position. Sometimes I smell unsportmanlike
behavior, but it's hard to judge against something that is allowed by
the rules.

Maybe self-oust should not be allowed. I don't like it at all, myself.
But I understand that a threat to self-oust can be put to good use (for
example, to give a player bargain leverage when a deal is being made
elsewhere on the table), so I'm not sure that outlawing it would be a
good idea.

> Or a simple, "no deals are acknowledged when only two Methuselahs remain -- at
> that point Methuselahs must play to win strictly from game state, not
> considering any prior deals".

I like this proposal a lot. I feel comfortable with it both as a player
and as a judge.

The only VP deal I've ever been in didn't work exactly as expected, and
by the time my prey had to roll over so I'd get my 2VP, the game state
was so that he could crash me in two minutes. I told him that I would
understand if he went ahead and killed me, but he chose to keep the
deal (after all, he only got his GW thanks to my help). It was all
legal, but how did it feel ridiculous to me.

If deals are automatically off once only two Methuselahs remain, I
think a lot of VP deals would not be made in the first place (because
the losing side would anticipate they seriously risk not getting
anything in the end), and some more would have to be "broken" when time
arrived. Sounds nice to me.

> But that would leave open the "help me oust Jim and I'll help you oust Bob, and
> then we can fight it out" deals.

This kind of deal may not be that bad, since it actually involves
playing. the. game. at some point. As long as it's both players' best
shot at the GW, I see nothing wrong with that.

I hope I've been able to express my point of view. I'm afraid that the
language barrier cuts short my ability to properly contribute in this
kind of conceptual debate.

Abraço,

Luiz Mello
Brazil VTES NC

Messages.Author: islando...@aol.com
Messages.Body:
> Perhaps (in addition or in place of a change to withdrawal rules), "Play to win"
> could be revisited to demand that self-preservation override any deals. That is,
> any "and I'll let you oust me" or "and I'll self-oust" deals would be disallowed
> (forcing their ilk into strangely-couched verbal contortions that hopefully can
> be sniffed out).

I like "self-preservation overrides any deals" once the game is down to
two players. I like it very much. It makes the game look a lot more
like it's a card game than a word game.

> Or a simple, "no deals are acknowledged when only two Methuselahs remain -- at
> that point Methuselahs must play to win strictly from game state, not
> considering any prior deals".

Also good, IMO. I believe this and the above would be functionally
identical. I request a debate about any distinctions between the two.

> But that would leave open the "help me oust Jim and I'll help you oust Bob, and
> then we can fight it out" deals.

I was forced to reply, as soon as I read this line. You see, I offer
this sort of deal often. It is, in my opinion, the best sort of VP
deal available, since it's limited in scope. You get help ousting your
prey, but then you still get the excitement of playing out an endgame
once you reach the endgame. I think any solution which prevents "Let's
agree upon how all VPs will be allocated this game," but still allows
"let's help each other get VPs and then play an endgame to determine a
winner" would be a good solution.

> > I think the best solution is to change the tournament structure
> > (especially at big tournaments) to more strongly encourage game wins
> > over VPs.

There already exists a format which strongly encourages GWs over VPs:
the 80+ player tournament. I enjoyed that format; table dealing for
1VP was much less common. I did not think it was necessary to
introduce the 2-day format in the first place as I felt I could
reasonably make the finals in the existing format.

But I digress. I think the only practical way to value GWs strongly
over VPs is to make certain that at least 4 of the 5 players in the
finals will need 2GW in order to be there--but it seems the general
consensus is that that sucks. So even though I disagree with the
consensus view, I believe it's a losing battle, so I won't advocate
"big enough championship that you need 2GW to make the finals."
Instead I think we should address the type of deal directly.

---------------------

I believe reducing withdrawal VPs to 0.5 is a good thing, but not
mainly in order to stop table dealing. (I advocate this mostly because
it prevents "There's 5 minutes left, let's all withdraw.") I believe
any fix which attempts to lessen the great number of table splits in
tournaments will need to target players' behavior directly, as opposed
to increasing the value of GWs or adjusting the value of withdrawal
VPs. Adding a rule that players can't willingly oust themselves as
part of a deal, mandating play to win over honoring a deal once the
table reaches 2 players, or simply stating that deals involving the
final state of VPs at a table are illegal deals inherently would all
achieve that end.

-- Brian

Messages.Author: atomweaver
Messages.Body:
LSJ <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in
news:tNAbh.17140$9v5....@newssvr29.news.prodigy.net:

> Or a simple, "no deals are acknowledged when only two Methuselahs
> remain -- at that point Methuselahs must play to win strictly from
> game state, not considering any prior deals".
>

The "Two Meths enter, one Meth leaves" variant on deal-making. I like
this option the best so far. Logically, ecumenically, and thematically
sound.
It always struck me that, other than the (effective!) stigma against
deal-breaking, once a game is down to two players an all-out struggle
for the win is the only "real" way to fulfill Play-to-Win (at that
point). The provision that you "can" honor a deal is a significant
aspect of what enables the stigma against deal-breaking. This
suggestion circumvents that aspect of deal-making neatly, as the new
rule would require you to play your hardest to win until the bitter
final resolution of the end game.

I see the possibility of limiting the duration of table talk per round
somewhat, too. If players know that they have to leave enough time at
the end to fully play out the end-game with whomever they're dealing
with, it means that they have to watch their use of time a little more
in the earlier rounds.
Due to that, I'd watch for tables with heavy negotiation to timeout
more often in the early era of the implementation of this rule, until
table-talkers get a better feel for how much end-game time they'll need.
After that, it shoudl settle down to its usual frequency, perhaps even
less frequent than now, as there would eventually be somewhat less
impetus to negotiate exhaustively...

> But that would leave open the "help me oust Jim and I'll help you oust
> Bob, and then we can fight it out" deals.
>

A point in its favor. Deals are certianly a part of VTES, and need to
remain so. This change would just limit them somewhat in the endbame,
to further enforce the idea that Playing to Win is primary...

A thing which might happen, is that players on the side of the "help

me oust Jim and I'll help you oust Bob, and then we can fight it out"

which involves the greater investment of resources may be left in a
weaker position in the end-game. This might be leveraged into a "wink-
wink" unspoken losing deal, but that circumstance would probably be as
easy to spot as any other surreptitious avoidance of the letter of the
rule. Something to look for in judging, maybe...

DaveZ
Atom Weaver

I think it makes a difference. In most smaller tournaments 1 or 2 GWs
are enough to make the final. The VPs are important in that case.
Players might be desperate enogh to not accept deals in which they get
only GW and 3 VPs. It might give players more incentive to strive go
for more points if possible, instead of stopping and letting the other
player collect the rest of the VPs.

If one player has already 1 GW and 4 VPs made "within", and in another
round with another player who is going to need a GW but has, say, 2 VPs
"without", to possibly make it to the final, a GW with 3 VPs would not
be enough. So a table split deal would not be that easy, and perhaps he
would play more aggressivly towards a sweep.

say, it would be a step in the right direction.

> extra VPs in exchange for securing the otherwise-in-question GW in both scenarios.

Dealing away extra VPs could make them cost their place in the final.
Players are greedy. :)

I would like to see those 3 components implemented:

1. Withdrawal automatically fails.
2. When down to 2 players, must play to win and deals can not be
honored.
3. Introducing VPs made during a GW, and those without as 2nd
tiebreaker, 3rd tiebreaker is still TPs.

I think no single point above will alleviate the problem enough, but
together, this might lead to a strengthening of the prey/predator
relationship without abolishing deals, which are in the nature of the
game.

I hope I have been clear on this subject as English is not my mother
tongue.

Carl

Messages.Author: Ben Swainbank
Messages.Body:
Peter D Bakija wrote:
>I am vastly more in favor of concrete, objective
> tweaks to the rules (i.e. removal of the Withdrawl rule, at least in
> tournaments, where it isn't needed for its intended purpose anyway)
> than subjective tweaks that require *more* judgement from judges (i.e.
> adjusting what is or is not a legal deal in the game).
>

Sure. But why not do do both? Change Withdraw so there's not "VP
incentive" to do it - make it worth 0, or .5 of go away AND add the
rule that Play to Win means that last 2 Methuselah can have or make
deals.

The new rule may have some enforcement issues, or it may not be so
hard. The important thing is that most players don't want to cheat.
They want to play. Under the current rules a smart, rule-following
player is going to try and carve up the table. Offer withdraws,
rollover deals, whatever it takes to maximize VP. That's playing the
game by the rules.

Add the no endgame deals rule. Now it take 2 players willing to cheat
in a sneaky way, and they mostly have to set it up in front of other
players. Imagine we have A->B->C.

A: "C, help me oust B, and I'll roll over."
B: "Hey! You can't make that deal."
A: "Right... C, if my prey was to get ousted, I might, hypothetically,
tap myself out and transfer down to 1 pool."
C: "Sorry dude. Play the game."

-Ben Swainbank

> > I think the best solution is to change the tournament structure
> > (especially at big tournaments) to more strongly encourage game wins
> > over VPs.
>

> Perhaps, but what would the substance of such a change look like?

Just tossing out ideas, here:
A) If you don't earn a GW, reduce your VP total for that game to 0.
TPs still count, though.

B) For 2-day events, make the cut-off be X players, or the lowest
ranked player with 1 GW, whichever is higher (rounded to nearest 5.)

C) If you earn 2 VPs and someone else gets the GW, you get 1 VP
instead.

I've only very briefly thought through the effects of A, but I'm
guessing it's not really a good idea. It seems like it may encourage
too many decks that win big or flop big. Then again, it would
discourage table split deals pretty significantly, so maybe it would be
good.

>From my single experience at a 2-day event, idea B would definitely
have eliminated a lot of the table split deals in day 1 of the NAC this
year. Also, I think this could be easily implemented without any major
negative consequences.

C directly addresses 3-2 (or now, 2.5-2) table splits by making the
losing end of the deal less appealing. It does allow for a 2.5 - 1.5
table split by simply agreeing to a draw when it's heads up, so you
could add:
C2) And, if you earn 1.5 VPs and someone else got 2.5 VPs or more, you
get 1 VP instead.
C3) And, if you earn 1.5 VPs, and someone else got 2 VPs and another
person got 1 VP, you get 1 VP instead.

C3 covers the case of:
D ousts E
B ousts C
A and C make a deal to oust B and let C withdraw (giving A the GW.)
A ousts B
then C withdraws for 1.5 VPs total. Turns out it's only 1 VP.

And C3 doesn't hurt the case of:
B ousts C
B ousts D
A ousts B
game times out

Have a good weekend,
Ira

Maybe - but it destroys what I've always thought was a rather good
balance between the advantages of playing at a 4-player table vs.
a 5-player table. At the 4-player table, you compete with one fewer
players for the game win, which is no small difference. I actually
think the 5-player table is already the worse deal, even though the
potential exists for grabbing another VP. If you were to do the
above, it would reverse the 5-player table advantage: a 4-player

less VP. I don't see how switching to the percentage formula is
going to make much difference one way or another.

Messages.Author: lysan...@excite.com
Messages.Body:
I apologise if this results in some form of a double post. I found
this thread originally on another forum, and posted a response to it
there. I thought it may have crossposted here, but since the post
hasnt shown up yet that might not have been the case. The other forum
also appears to be quite dead. So here it is again.

Please note that I will not be able to participate in any discussions
for the next two weeks due to a work trip abroad.

-------------------------
I played a storyline tournament recently under the new withdrawal and
endgame tournament rules. Every game I played in still had shameless
table splitting going on. Even though the 'play to win' rule has good
intent, it is not very enforceable. There is nothing to prevent a
player in the end rolling over and dying without a fight (or at least
pretending to squirm a little), and there is nothing to prevent both
players taking their time and playing for the time limit.

My suggestion, for all its worth is this. Remove VPs from any
tournament standing consideration. Players may earn Ranking Points and
Game Wins only. A GW is the primary consideration in qualification for
the final table, with Ranking points used as the tie breakers. A
Ranking point is awarded in this manner:

4 player games
- if your prey or predator earned the GW = 0 ranking points.
- if your grandpredator/grandprey earned the GW = 1 ranking point

5 player games
- if your prey or predator earned the GW = 0 ranking points.
- if your grandprey earned the GW = 1 ranking point.
- if your grandpredator earned the GW = 0.5 ranking point.

(in the above, prey or predator refers to the original prey and
predator as of the beginning of the game)

Finally, if a game ends in a draw, the players involved in the draw
each receive a proportional fraction of 0.6 GW. For example, if two
players draw then they each receive 0.3 GW for the final score. If
three players draw they each receive 0.2 GW for the final score.

This means that:

a) players must win rounds to move up the tournament.
b) if you cannot win, the absolute worst thing you can do is allow
your prey or your predator to win the game. This means you will always
be trying to hurt your prey as much as possible, while trying your
utmost best to live against the assaults of your predator.
c) victory points are used only for calculation of the GW, so cutting
deals for individual VPs during a game is worthless, unless it will
somehow help you attain the GW.
d) a draw is better than losing, but no amount of draws will ever
equal a full GW.

It may sound complicated to calculate ranking points during play, but
I am sure a modification to the tournament tracker would be easy
enough.

My question is how were these deals made? Making table-split deal has
always required a high degree of trust. Now, you can't really announce
that you're a man of your word and won't break the deal. Doing so
would involve announcing your intent to cheat.

So, the deal has to be offered and accepted in some kind of nudge-wink
way, such the other players getting screwed don't suspect anything and
call a judge over. Then the would-be rollover deal makers have to
trust the other party to honorable enough to keep the deal AND
dishonorable enough to cheat at the game to do so.

How are these "shameless" deals being made?

Messages.Author: lysan...@excite.com
Messages.Body:
On Jan 30, 10:50 pm, "Ben Swainbank" <bswainb...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> How are these "shameless" deals being made?

Shameless was a bad word to use. Here is the full tournament report:

I was playing a very average Tzimisce deck modelled on the 3rd ed
starter. There were 21-24 players in the tournament

First round I was bleeding a special deck. Special in that it was a
pure master card deck, with a 2 pt gangrel and a 3 point !Brujah as
the only minions the deck would pull out (they did nothing, just sat
there to be thrown in the way of huge bleeds). The deck was completely
innefective, and there seemed to be no thought put into how to oust
its prey. Shame, because the guy playing it was a very cool guy and
really he should have known better. This disgrace of a deck was
sitting behind a !Toreador deck (notice I didnt say it was bleeding
the !Toreador). The !Toreador was in turn bleeding a set 1 Nos deck,
who was my predator. So a 4 player game.

The game went something like this:
Turn 1, everyone does some transfers. My prey pulls out a two pointer
gangrel. My grandprey pulls out a 4 pointer.
Turn 2, my predator pulls out a 7 pt Nos prince. I Pentex Subversion
the Nos and pull out Elizabeth the 5 pointer. My prey pulls out Jacob
Brag. I tell my grandprey to bleed my predator hard. Instead he
creates an embrace.
Turn 3, my predator can only do transfers. I do transfers onto Sha-
Ennu (the 11 pointer who was the only other decent vamp in my crypt),
and keep Elizabeth untapped in case my prey tries to burn off the
Pentex. My prey plays a Society of Leopold on the newly created
embrace and burns it, pissing off my grandprey. My grandprey then has
his turn. I tell him to bleed my predator hard and get the edge. He
creates another embrace (sigh).
Turn 4, my predator does some transfers, and still only has the one
minion with the Pentex Subversion on it. I do transfers to Sha-Ennu
and sit pretty. My prey plays another Society of Leopold on the new
embrace, burning that one as well (note my prey is doing no more
transfers, as it is a deck full of masters). So here is where the true
skill of that table comes out. My grandprey has his turn. He starts
screaming at me, saying that he has had two minions burned already,
and that I am doing nothing against my prey. I point it out to him
that I am still pulling out my second minion, and that I have been
keeping my only minion untapped to guarantee him a free run on his
prey (by ensuring the Pentex is not burned off). Undeterred, he
declares that he will burn off the Pentex Subversion that is on his
preys only minion! I just didnt know what to say to that, considering
his predator was incapable of bleeding. He stealthed through the
action to burn the Pentex, and freed up his prey to come after me. As
soon as he did this he cut a deal with his prey to allow his prey a
table sweep in exchange for 0.5 VP!!! So now I had to hold off my
predator with heavy potence, stealth and votes (yes, a voting Nos
deck), and bleed through my preys 25 pool. The game carried on from
there. Eventually I managed to bleed through my prey, and managed to
bring my grandprey down to 1 pool. All the while I was fending off the
Nos voting deck, who had complete control of the storyline Cultist.
Died to the onslaught though, with only 1 VP to my name. In retrospect
I should have called a ref over and had him arbitrate over this,
though I dont think it would have helped. The VP bottom-feeder across
the table was quite content to play for 0.5-1 VP. I dont think the
thought of winning a tournament round actually occurred to him.

Second round - 5 player game. I was bleeding an EuroBrujah deck, who
in turn was bleeding a Ventrue deck, followed by a !Malk deck,
followed by an Akunanse deck. I pulled out Elizabeth, my prey pulled
out Constanza. Next turn I tried to pull out a retainer. My prey
blocked it with a second tradition and levelled my vamp in one strike
(she didnt have superior viscissitude, so I didnt really do anything
in return). That left the shitty 4 pointer, a 9 pointer and an 11
pointer in my uncontrolled region. I pulled out the 4 pointer to hold
off the horde until I could pull out one of the big vamps. In the
meantime my predator obtained control of the cultist and bled me for
all he was worth. By the time my next minion came out I was down to 3
pool and it was game over. In the same turn my prey ousted my
grandprey. There were now 3 players left in the game, two of them with
1 VP each. The Akunanse deck was in a commanding position. I left the
game area at this point, but found out later that the table was
subsequently split up by a deal, with the victory going to the
Akunanse player. I dont know the details of the deal though.

Third round I was bleeding a Tremere deck, who was bleeding a Ventrue
deck, who was behind the master card deck from the first round, and
who in turn was (not) bleeding my predator - a Nos voting deck. So a 5
player game.

Here is a description of the Nos voting deck: essentially high
capacity set 1 Nos vamps, all with votes and typically with fortitude.
The only fortitude card he played was freak drive. There were an
incredible amount of votes in the deck, but they were all either
parity shifts of kine resources contested. Heaps of Legendary
Vampires, and the most minimal amount of stealth. Absolutely zero
combat or combat avoidance.

Due to the lack of stealth in his deck, I did a fairly good job of
locking up my predator with my Tzimisce deck, even though he in turn
had no predator. Not that it mattered, because a few turns later he
lost voting dominance to my prey and had a 100% innefective deck. My
prey, the Tremere player, also had no combat in the deck. He knew that
if I caught any one of his minions that there was nothing he could do,
so he did the only other thing he could: he lunged all out with masses
of dominate. My grandprey, being incredibly wise, chose Arika as the
first vamp to pull out. By the time he pulled out Arika he was down to
2 pool, rolled over and died. Meanwhile I was layering in 5-6 pool of
bleed into my prey every turn, none of which was blocked. Next in line
was the master card deck, but given the amount of pool he had the
Tremere player seriously hesitated. This is where the panic settled
in. My prey knew that he was going to die before long, since he
couldnt afford to block my vamps. My predator was locked up by fear of
my intercept and by the inability to pass his votes. So the two of
them organised to kill me by using the middle cultist and by voting
together whenever possible to oust me. They arranged to withdraw after
both me and my grandpredator were eliminated. The referee ruled this
was ok for both of them to do because: a) my predator was not going to
get any VPs unless the deal was made, and b) my prey would get the
table win even if he let my predator get the VP for ousting me and the
0.5 VP for withdrawing. Two turns later I got caught without intercept
and wore votes plus stealthy cultist bleed, knocking me out. My grand
predator of course could do nothing (since he only had master cards).

It never occurred to my predator (or to the referree) that if he just
waited until I killed the Tremere player, that I would also have to
bleed through the gigantic amouont of pool the master card deck had.
This would take considerable time, during which my predator would have
had voting dominance and could have potentially gotten the better of
me. One could argue there was no chance of that of course, though in
all my years of playing I have found that there is always a chance to
win as long as you still live.

-------------------------------------

Things will probably get better as people get used to the new rules I
guess. What I was hoping for with my suggestion was to create a
system whereby actively going after your prey and trying your hardest
to stop your predator from ousting you becomes something that is
actively encouraged by the rules.
