Messages.Author: lysan...@excite.com
Messages.Body:
On Jan 30, 11:14 pm, James Coupe <j...@zephyr.org.uk> wrote:
> So, if I can't win, my optimum strategy is to run backwards and hit my
> predator so hard that he dies in a heap and my grand-predator rolls the
> table.

Interesting way of looking at it. A player could certainly do that.
I looked at it a bit differently:

- Since ranking points would be allocated based purely on seating
relative to the winning deck, your hard work going backwards and
trying to oust your predator would earn you a grand total of 1 ranking
point. One player in each table of the tournament round would also
earn this same ranking point based purely on their seating. Your
optimum strategy if you absolutely know you cant win would actually be
to go for the draw, and you should scheme, manipulate and bully your
way into that draw.
- If you know you cant win, how come you can try to oust your predator
but not your prey? How is that very much different to a player
attempting to hurt back a predator who has hurt him too much during a
game?
- If you hurt your predator too much, and he has the same sort of
attitude, might he not try to do the same to his predator and thus
help your prey to win?

In a five player game I suggested that you earn only 0.5 ranking point
for letting your grandpredator win, while you'd get 1 ranking point
for being in a table in which your grandprey wins, so going back and
hurting your predator does not help you in any way. In a four player
game if you go forwards and hurt your prey, your grandprey should also
in theory have an easier time hitting your predator, so even in that
scenario I dont see the need to view ousting your predator as an
optimum strategy. Your optimum strategy is always to win the game,
followed by generating a draw, followed far behind by destroying your
prey and allowing your grandprey to sweep.

Is there are problem with the current rules? Are they difficult to
arbitrate? Do they encourage players to maximise safe VPs at the
expense of the possible GW? If not then you are absolutely right, and
there is no reason to change the tournament rules at all. In that
case my proposition can remain strictly as a thought exercise to
stimulate discussion. Iff there is a problem, then at some point
alternatives should be considered. I have proposed one such
alternative. My suggestion recommends removing the incentive to split
a table to scrounge VPs each round, and instead allocates points based
purely on seating relative to the winner. Anyone could get ranking
points, so the players that will consistently do better will be the
players that consistently strive to the very end for the GW. As an
added suggestion, VPs could still be important for VEKN ratings. This
means that performance in a tournament in not dependant on individual
VPs, but that individual VPs would still affect a players overall
rating.

I have to go. Will be back in two weeks.

I like the system from a purely hypothetical point of view. However, I

> a) players must win rounds to move up the tournament.

Technically, this is achieved by the GW rule (a.k.a. the "death to
forward motion" rule as I often like to refer to it out of more
hatred for walls than weenie swarm decks).

> b) if you cannot win, the absolute worst thing you can do is allow
> your prey or your predator to win the game. This means you will always
> be trying to hurt your prey as much as possible, while trying your
> utmost best to live against the assaults of your predator.

As others pointed out, in some cases you are better off giving the

2 predators loses).

> c) victory points are used only for calculation of the GW, so cutting

> somehow help you attain the GW.

As said by others, if you have them, track them, you might as well use
them unless there is something much better (in which case you would
have and track that other thing, instead, most likely).

> d) a draw is better than losing, but no amount of draws will ever
> equal a full GW.

Similar in the current system.

> It may sound complicated to calculate ranking points during play, but
> I am sure a modification to the tournament tracker would be easy
> enough.

Ok, here's the catch. The main problem with the current tournament rules
is not what they stand for technically. I mean, look at it: the aim is
to oust your prey. You get VP for ousting your prey. Nothing is as
direct as that.

The main problem is with the ambiguity introduced by the political aspect
of the game - which is pretty much supported by the game, by the way -
that makes it rather hard in cases to judge whether a player is well
within the boundaries of sportsmanship or just a tadbit outside of them.

It takes a competent and attentive judge to enforce the spirit of the
rules. Unfortunately (?) the very same prowesses that make one a
successful negotiator in game also tend to enable one to be successful
at bending the spirit of the rules in a subtle way.

Messages.Author: wumpus
Messages.Body:
Howdy,

<snip generous details>

> First round ... As

> soon as he did this he cut a deal with his prey to allow his prey a
> table sweep in exchange for 0.5 VP!!!

How was this supposed to work? Presumably the deal was that he
('bottom-feeder') would assist your predator (his prey) in ousting the
rest of the table and then be allowed to withdraw (for 0.5 VP)? The
problem being that all deals are off once you and your prey are gone,
and now your predator _has to_ try to oust bottom-feeder, which really
shouldn't be too tricky for him, from the sound of things...

Which should make this a clearly pointless and/or illegal deal to
begin with. And that's without even considering how clearly non-play-
to-win both your prey and bottom-feeder's play is, as described. In
the case of the bottom-feeder, you can't just decide to give up any
chance to win because you don't like how the game is proceeding. In
the case of the 'do-nothing' deck (Was this deck even legal? What
clan was it?), it's pathologically unsportsmanlike to come to a
tournament with a deck that cannot win - you are wasting not only your
own time, but everyone else's.

> In retrospect
> I should have called a ref over and had him arbitrate over this,
> though I dont think it would have helped. The VP bottom-feeder across
> the table was quite content to play for 0.5-1 VP. I dont think the
> thought of winning a tournament round actually occurred to him.

This is, indeed, precisely what judges are for. If you can't count on
your judge to rule correctly in a situation like this, then why even
have a judge?

While the judge's options would be limited if the player(s) in
question refuse to cooperate (He then has to eject them - yuck!), in
this case it should have sufficed to point out that the deal was
plainly illegal and, in fact, _could not_ be adhered to at precisely
the point when it would be important to the bottom-feeder (i.e. when
it came time to withdraw), by explicit V:EKN rules! At that point,
bottom-feeder should recognize that the only way he's going to get any
VP at all is to go forward (and/or make deals with someone who isn't
his prey).

> Second round ... I left the

> game area at this point, but found out later that the table was
> subsequently split up by a deal, with the victory going to the
> Akunanse player. I dont know the details of the deal though.

This all sounded kosher. Brutal, but kosher.

> Third round ... My prey knew that he was going to die before long, since he

> couldnt afford to block my vamps. My predator was locked up by fear of
> my intercept and by the inability to pass his votes. So the two of
> them organised to kill me by using the middle cultist and by voting
> together whenever possible to oust me. They arranged to withdraw after
> both me and my grandpredator were eliminated. The referee ruled this
> was ok for both of them to do because: a) my predator was not going to
> get any VPs unless the deal was made, and b) my prey would get the
> table win even if he let my predator get the VP for ousting me and the
> 0.5 VP for withdrawing.

It's certainly legal for your predator and prey to deal you out of the
game in these circumstances. It's good play, even. What they can't
do anymore is to agree to withdraw. That's explicitly not allowed.
All deals are off when you reach the two-player endgame. So this is a
legal deal for you prey - who would get 2.5 VP and a game win out of
it - but not for your predator, who would end up with 1.5 VP. When it
comes down to just the two of them, they _must_ play to win, which,
for your predator, means attempting to oust. (And it hardly seems
worth 0.5 VP to not even try to oust at that point anyway.) I suppose
your predator could claim a 'lost' position at that point, but it'd be
hard to explain why your prey should let him withdraw if he's in a
'lost' position...

I don't know how the judge missed the whole 'all deals are off in the
two-player endgame' update to the V:EKN rules; his ruling seems
clearly incorrect. Of course, a better ruling probably would have had
the same impact on your game - being ousted. It just would've forced
your predator and prey to actually fight out the endgame (with a time-
out achieving the same result anyway).

Hope that helps,
Alex
